title: Sentence Structure & Types
description: Learn sentence types and structure for Grade 6: declarative, interrogative, imperative and exclamatory sentences, subject and predicate, objects and complements — with practice and tests.

topics.title: Four Types of Sentences by Purpose
topics.concept:
Sentences are classified by what they do:

  • Declarative (statement): tells something and ends with a full stop. She plays the violin.
  • Interrogative (question): asks something and ends with a question mark. Does she play the violin?
  • Imperative (command/request): tells someone to do something; the subject 'you' is usually hidden. Close the door. Please sit down.
  • Exclamatory: expresses sudden, strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark. How beautiful the garden is!

examples.problem: Name the type: What a wonderful surprise!
examples.solution: Exclamatory — it shows strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark.

examples.problem: Name the type: Please pass the salt.
examples.solution: Imperative — it makes a polite request; the subject 'you' is understood.

topics.title: Subject, Predicate, Objects & Complement
topics.concept:
Every sentence divides into a subject (who/what) and a predicate (what is said about it).

  • The tall boy | scored a goal.

Inside the predicate we may find:

  • Direct object — receives the action (what/whom?): She ate an apple.
  • Indirect object — to/for whom the action is done: He gave me a book.
  • Complement — completes the meaning after a linking verb: She is a doctor; the soup tastes salty.

Test for the subject: ask who? or what? before the verb.

examples.problem: Find subject and predicate: The children played in the park.
Find the direct and indirect objects: Mother gave Riya a gift.

recap: Subject = who/what; Predicate = what is said about it
Direct object receives the action; indirect object = to/for whom
A complement completes meaning after a linking verb

questions.q: 'The train arrived on time.' is:
questions.explanation: It states a fact — declarative.

questions.q: Which ends with a question mark?
questions.explanation: 'Are you ready?' is interrogative.

questions.q: 'Bring me some water.' is:
questions.explanation: It gives a command — imperative.

questions.q: In 'My brother reads books', the predicate is:
questions.explanation: 'reads books' tells what the subject does.

questions.q: 'How clever she is!' is:
questions.explanation: Strong feeling → exclamatory.

questions.q: In 'He gave her a rose', the indirect object is:
questions.explanation: 'her' = to whom — indirect object.

questions.q: The subject in 'Under the tree sat a dog' is:
questions.explanation: Ask 'who sat?' → 'a dog' is the subject.

questions.q: Which is a complement? 'The cake smells delicious.'
questions.explanation: 'delicious' completes the meaning after the linking verb.

questions.q: Change to interrogative: 'She can swim.'
questions.explanation: Put the helping verb first: 'Can she swim?'

questions.q: 'Wow, we won the cup!' is:
questions.explanation: It shows strong feeling — exclamatory.

questions.q: Which sentence is imperative?
questions.explanation: 'Be kind …' gives a command.

questions.q: In 'The boys play cricket', the direct object is:
questions.explanation: 'cricket' receives the action.

questions.q: Change to exclamatory: 'It is a very sad story.'
options: What a sad story it is!
questions.explanation: 'What a + adjective + noun!' makes it exclamatory.

questions.q: Identify the error: 'Please you bring the book.'
questions.explanation: An imperative drops the subject 'you'.

questions.q: Which sentence has an object complement?
questions.explanation: 'captain' completes the meaning of the object 'him' — an object complement.

questions.q: Change to assertive (declarative): 'How hardworking she is!'
questions.explanation: An exclamatory becomes an assertive with 'very'.

questions.q: Pick the correctly transformed negative: 'Everyone liked the film.'
questions.explanation: 'Everyone liked' = 'No one disliked' keeps the meaning.

questions.q: In 'The committee appointed her secretary', 'secretary' is:
questions.explanation: It renames the object 'her' — object complement.

questions.q: Rearrange into a question: 'the / where / did / keys / you / put'
options: Where did you put the keys?
Where you did put the keys?
Did where you put the keys?
Where put did you the keys?
questions.explanation: 'Where did you put the keys?' is correct.

questions.q: Change to imperative: 'You should respect your elders.'
questions.explanation: Drop 'You should' to form the command 'Respect your elders.'

outcomes: Identify the four types of sentences by purpose
Change a sentence between statement, question and negative

intro.en: A sentence is a group of words that expresses a complete thought. Every sentence has two essential parts: a subject (who or what we talk about) and a predicate (what is said about the subject). Sentences also come in four types depending on their purpose.
intro.hi: वाक्य (Sentence) शब्दों का वह समूह है जो एक पूरा विचार प्रकट करता है। हर वाक्य के दो मुख्य भाग होते हैं: उद्देश्य (subject) — जिसके बारे में बात हो, और विधेय (predicate) — जो उसके बारे में कहा जाए। उद्देश्य के अनुसार वाक्य चार प्रकार के होते हैं।

real_life.situation:
In one short chat you use every type:

You: The bus is late. (statement) Is it coming? (question) Please wait here. (command) What a long wait! (exclamation)
real_life.why: Each sentence does a different job — to tell, to ask, to order, to exclaim. Recognising the purpose helps you punctuate it correctly (full stop, question mark or exclamation mark).

quick_test.q: A sentence that gives a command is called:
quick_test.explanation: Imperative sentences give commands or requests (Open the door).

common_mistakes.note: A question must end with a question mark.
An exclamatory sentence ends with an exclamation mark.
In an imperative sentence the subject 'you' is understood and usually dropped.
The indirect object (me) comes before the direct object (a book).

reading.passage: The bell rang loudly. "Hurry up!" shouted the teacher. The students rushed to the hall. Who would win the quiz? Ria gave her team the final answer, and they cheered. What an exciting morning it was!

questions.q: Find an interrogative sentence in the passage.
questions.answer: "Who would win the quiz?" — it asks a question.

questions.q: Find an exclamatory sentence.
questions.answer: "What an exciting morning it was!" — it shows strong feeling.

questions.q: In 'Ria gave her team the final answer', name the indirect object.
questions.answer: her team — it tells to whom the answer was given.

micro_quiz.explanation: 'a pen' receives the action — direct object.
